query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Adding 0.2 atomic percent Mo to the as-cast, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will modify its microstructure to yield a better balance of strength and ductility, improve creep resistance at room temperature, and enhance corrosion resistance under high-temperature fluctuations.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform fine lamellar microstructure composed of coupled fcc (L12) and B2 phases.
generation.intervention: Introduce 0.2 at.% Mo through alloying during the melting and casting stage.
generation.conditions: Performance is aimed for fasteners exposed to cyclic thermal fluctuations (from room temperature up to approximately 700°C), long-term mechanical loading including room-temperature creep, and corrosive environments such as chloride-containing or other aggressive media.
generation.structural_mediator: Refinement and stabilization of the lamellar fcc/B2 morphology along with the possible formation of Mo-rich nano-precipitates that help arrest dislocation motion and inhibit phase instability.
generation.mechanism: The Mo addition is expected to shift the phase balance—either by stabilizing the ductile fcc phase or by precipitating a fine Mo-containing phase. These changes can lead to an increased yield strength and improved work hardening while maintaining or even enhancing ductility. Furthermore, Mo is known to improve corrosion resistance and high-temperature stability, which would mitigate issues from thermal cycling and long-term mechanical loading, including room-temperature creep.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Mo-alloyed variant is predicted to have an increase in yield and tensile strengths (improvements on the order of 3.6–34%) and enhanced fracture elongation (up to 0.9–2.9 times greater), along with lower creep rates and improved resistance to corrosion under fluctuating and high-temperature environments.
generation.baseline: The starting AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy in its uniform fine lamellar state, which has strength and plasticity below industry requirements for fastener applications.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under conventional industrial processing and testing conditions for eutectic high-entropy alloys, with expected performance benefits maintained up to around 700°C and in environments typical for corrosive fastener applications. Performance in very different processing scales or extreme conditions outside these ranges may vary.
generation.uncertainty: While previous studies indicate beneficial effects of Mo addition in similar systems, the exact magnitude of improvements—as well as the potential influence of processing parameters and Mo distribution—remains uncertain and requires experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples: one set with the standard composition and one with an additional 0.2 at.% Mo incorporated during casting. Process both sets under identical thermomechanical conditions. Subject the samples to cyclic thermal testing (room temperature up to 700°C), prolonged mechanical loading including room-temperature creep tests, and corrosion testing in chloride-containing solutions.
measurements: Tensile yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation at fracture
Creep rate at room temperature under sustained load
Corrosion rate and potential in corrosive media
Microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM/TEM, phase analysis) to detect changes in phase proportions and any Mo-rich precipitate formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-alloyed samples fail to show statistically significant improvements (at the 95% confidence level) in mechanical properties (strength and ductility), reduced creep rates, and/or enhanced corrosion resistance compared to the baseline samples—or if deleterious phases develop that adversely affect performance—the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs.
